bank.q: What does the name "Mesopotamia" mean?
bank.why: Mesopotamia means "between rivers," referring to the Tigris and Euphrates.
bank.hint: The region is defined by two famous waterways.

bank.q: Which two rivers give Mesopotamia its name?
bank.why: Mesopotamia lies "between rivers": the Tigris and the Euphrates.
bank.hint: Neither river runs through Egypt or India.

bank.q: Which modern-day areas does Mesopotamia cover?
bank.a: Iraq, eastern Syria and southeastern Turkey
d: Egypt, Sudan and the northern coast of Libya
Greece, Cyprus and the western coast of Turkey
bank.why: The slides place Mesopotamia in modern-day Iraq, eastern Syria and southeastern Turkey.

bank.q: Is Mesopotamia a civilization or an era?
bank.a: A geographical region where several civilizations developed
d: A single civilization founded and ruled by the Sumerians
An era of history that ended with the Old Babylonian Period
One city-state built on the banks of the Tigris River
bank.why: Mesopotamia refers primarily to a geographical region. The Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians all developed there.
bank.hint: Several peoples lived there over thousands of years.

bank.q: Which list names civilizations that developed in Mesopotamia?
bank.why: The slides list the Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians.
bank.hint: Pick the list with no Egyptians, Greeks or Romans.

bank.q: Which region does the lecture call the "cradle of the world's earliest civilization"?
bank.why: Mesopotamia is described as the cradle of the world's earliest civilization.

bank.q: During which period did the earliest Mesopotamian medical practice appear?
bank.why: The earliest medical practice dates to the Uruk Period (c. 4000 to 3100 BCE).
bank.hint: It is the oldest period named in the lecture.

bank.q: In which period did Mesopotamian medicine become a well-established profession, with knowledge recorded in written texts?
bank.why: By the Old Babylonian Period (c. 1894 to 1595 BCE), medicine was an established profession with written texts.

bank.q: What are the approximate dates of the Uruk Period?
bank.why: Uruk Period: c. 4000 to 3100 BCE. (1894 to 1595 BCE is Old Babylonian; 3300 to 525 BCE is Egyptian medicine.)

bank.q: What are the approximate dates of the Old Babylonian Period?
bank.why: Old Babylonian Period: c. 1894 to 1595 BCE.
bank.hint: It falls in the second millennium BCE.

bank.q: Most of what is known about Mesopotamian medicine comes from which source?
bank.why: Cuneiform tablets recorded symptoms, treatments, prescriptions and other medical knowledge.
bank.hint: The writing was pressed into clay.

bank.q: In Mesopotamian spiritual medicine, illness was believed to involve what?
d: An imbalance of the four humors
bank.why: Spiritual medicine held that illness involved gods, demons or spirits.

bank.q: Which of these belongs to Mesopotamian SPIRITUAL medicine?
bank.why: Spiritual medicine used prayers, incantations, spells, amulets, astrology, divination and omens. The other options are practical medicine.

bank.q: Which of these was part of Mesopotamian PRACTICAL medicine?
d: Incantations, spells and prayers to the gods
Astrology and divination by the priests
bank.why: Practical medicine included herbal remedies, medicines, wound treatment, surgery, dentistry and cleanliness.

bank.q: What do the slides mean by "Mesopotamian medicine was not purely magic"?
bank.a: Healers also used practical treatments like herbs, wound care and surgery
d: Mesopotamians rejected every religious explanation of illness
Magic was banned by the Old Babylonian kings in favor of surgery
Only priests were allowed to treat the sick, and only with spells
bank.why: Mesopotamian medicine combined spiritual medicine with practical medicine.
bank.hint: Two kinds of medicine existed side by side.

bank.q: Mesopotamians used willow bark (and plants like myrtle) as what?
d: An anesthetic drink taken with wine before surgery
A disinfectant for cleaning surgical tools
A treatment for fever after childbirth
bank.why: Willow bark served as a natural painkiller and anti-inflammatory.

bank.q: Mesopotamian medicine had no pills. How were remedies usually applied instead?
bank.why: There were no pills; remedies were applied as poultices.

bank.q: Who was the Sumerian goddess of healing and the principal deity associated with medicine?
bank.why: Gula was the Sumerian goddess of healing who guided doctors and dentists.

bank.q: Which other names does the lecture associate with Gula?
bank.why: The slides link Gula with Ninkarrak and Ninisinna.
bank.hint: Both names begin with "Nin", and neither is her son.

bank.q: Ninazu, the son of Gula, was associated with which of the following?
bank.a: Healing, serpents, transformation and the underworld
d: Agriculture, tea, farming and herbal medicine
Childbirth, fertility, pregnancy and women's health
Dreams, temples, pilgrimages and sacred sleep
bank.why: Ninazu was linked to healing, serpents, transformation and the underworld.
bank.hint: Think about the modern medical symbol.

bank.q: The rod intertwined with serpents, now associated with the medical profession, is linked in the lecture source to which figure?
bank.why: The slides link the serpent rod to Ninazu, the god of healing and serpents.
bank.hint: A Mesopotamian god, son of a goddess.

bank.q: What was an Asu in Mesopotamia?
bank.a: A practical physician using herbs, physical treatments and wound care
d: A spiritual healer who used incantations, spells and divination
The goddess who guided doctors and dentists in treating illness
A demon believed to cause illness, driven away by rituals
bank.why: The Asu treated illness with practical, empirical methods.
bank.hint: The shorter name is the practical healer.

bank.q: What was an Asipu in Mesopotamia?
bank.a: A religious healer using prayers, incantations, spells and divination
d: A practical physician who treated wounds with herbs and poultices
A scribe who copied prescriptions onto cuneiform tablets
A healer who set fractures and pulled teeth by hand
bank.why: The Asipu performed rituals to drive away supernatural causes of illness.

bank.q: A Mesopotamian family believes the demon Lamashtu is making their child sick. Which healer would they most likely call?
bank.why: The Asipu performed rituals to drive away or protect patients from supernatural causes of illness such as Lamashtu.

bank.q: A Mesopotamian laborer has a deep cut on his arm. A healer cleans it and applies an herbal poultice. Which kind of healer is this?
bank.why: The Asu used practical methods such as herbal remedies and wound care.
bank.hint: The treatment is physical, not spiritual.

bank.q: Ancient Egyptian medicine developed along the Nile during roughly which period?
bank.why: Egyptian medicine developed along the Nile from about 3300 to 525 BCE.

bank.q: Where did Egyptians record their knowledge of diseases, anatomy, medicines, treatments and surgery?
bank.why: Egyptians recorded medical knowledge in medical papyri.
bank.hint: Made from a reed that grows along the Nile.

bank.q: How does the lecture describe the Egyptian healthcare system?
bank.a: It combined clinical treatment with religious and magical practices
d: It relied only on spells, prayers and rituals for every illness
It rejected religion entirely in favor of surgery and herbs
It was run only by foreign Greek physicians trained in Athens
bank.why: Egyptian healthcare combined clinical procedures with spells and rituals for illnesses believed to have supernatural causes.

bank.q: Who served as a high official under Pharaoh Djoser and became one of the most famous medical figures of ancient Egypt?
bank.why: Imhotep was a high official under Pharaoh Djoser.

bank.q: Imhotep served as a high official under which pharaoh?
bank.why: Imhotep served under Pharaoh Djoser.

bank.q: Why is the Rosetta Stone important to the history of Egyptian medicine?
bank.a: Its translation made it possible to read Egypt's medical records
d: It is the oldest Egyptian surgical textbook ever found
It lists Imhotep's prescriptions for treating fractures
It describes the first Egyptian vaccine against plague
bank.why: Translating the Rosetta Stone let scholars understand Egyptian writing and eventually interpret medical records.
bank.hint: It is a key to a language.

bank.q: In what year was the Rosetta Stone translated?
bank.why: The Rosetta Stone was translated in 1822.

bank.q: Which papyrus contains prescriptions and information on general medicine, diseases, medications and magical treatments?
bank.why: The Ebers Papyrus covers prescriptions, general medicine and magical treatments.

bank.q: Which papyrus focuses on injuries, wounds, fractures, anatomy, patient examination and surgical treatment?
bank.why: The Edwin Smith Papyrus is the injury and surgery papyrus.

bank.q: Which papyrus discusses women's health, fertility, pregnancy and gynecological conditions?
bank.why: The Kahun Gynecological Papyrus deals with women's health.
bank.hint: Its full name gives it away.

bank.q: A historian wants to learn how Egyptian physicians examined and treated a broken arm. Which papyrus should they read first?
bank.why: Fractures, wounds and surgical treatment are the focus of the Edwin Smith Papyrus.

bank.q: A researcher studying how ancient Egyptians handled fertility problems and pregnancy would look mainly at which source?
bank.why: The Kahun Gynecological Papyrus discusses fertility, pregnancy and gynecological conditions.

bank.q: Which of these is NOT one of the Egyptian medical papyri named in the lecture?
bank.why: The papyri named are Ebers, Edwin Smith, Kahun, Hearst and London. Charaka is the Indian author of the Charaka Samhita.

bank.q: Which best describes "organized medical practice" in ancient Egypt?
bank.a: Physicians examined, diagnosed, predicted outcomes and prescribed treatment
d: Healers relied only on spells and amulets, never on examination
Priests timed every treatment with the movement of the stars
Barbers performed all surgery in public squares for a fee
bank.why: Egyptian physicians followed an organized process from examination to prescription.
bank.hint: It sounds like a modern consultation.

bank.q: Egyptian medicinal remedies were made from which ingredients?
bank.a: Herbs and plants, honey, milk, animal fat, minerals and metals
d: Mercury, sulfur and salt prepared by early chemists
Cowpox fluid and bacteria weakened in a laboratory
Cannabis, monkshood and datura mixed into wine
bank.why: Egyptians used herbs, plants, honey, milk, animal fat, minerals and metals for illnesses, wounds and skin conditions.
bank.hint: Mostly natural plant and household ingredients.

bank.q: Why did Egyptian physicians sometimes combine treatments with spells, prayers, rituals and amulets?
bank.a: Some illnesses were believed to have supernatural causes
d: The pharaoh had banned practical medicine for commoners
Spells were thought to be the only way to clean tools
Only priests were allowed to read the medical papyri
bank.why: Religious and magical practices were used for illnesses believed to have supernatural causes.
bank.hint: What did they believe caused some illnesses?

bank.q: According to the lecture, which areas did Egyptian physicians understand or perform?
bank.a: Anatomy, dentistry, wound care and fracture treatment
d: Blood circulation through a closed system pumped by the heart
Germ theory, pasteurization and laboratory vaccines
bank.why: Egyptians understood anatomy, diseases, dentistry and medicine preparation, and performed wound care and fracture treatment.
bank.hint: Only one option fits the ancient world.

bank.q: What was ancient Greece's main contribution to the direction of medicine?
bank.a: It moved medicine toward observation and natural explanations of disease
d: It replaced observation with dreams in the temples of Asclepius
It introduced chemical remedies like mercury, sulfur and iron
It proved that germs, not humors, are the cause of disease
bank.why: Greece shifted medicine toward rational observation and natural explanations, and helped establish clinical documentation.

bank.q: What characterized Greek medicine in the 5th century BC?
bank.a: Physicians studied symptoms and outcomes, while temple healing continued
d: Temple healing was outlawed so that only physicians could treat
Physicians relied only on sacred dreams to choose treatments
Medicine was based entirely on astrology and celestial charts
bank.why: Physicians increasingly studied the body and outcomes, though religious and temple healing continued.
bank.hint: Both kinds of healing existed together.

bank.q: People visited sanctuaries such as Epidaurus to seek cures through sacred dreams. Which healing figure were these sanctuaries for?
bank.why: Asclepius was a major healing figure; Epidaurus was one of his sanctuaries.
bank.hint: A legendary healer, not a historical physician.

bank.q: What were the Asclepieia?
bank.a: Temples of Asclepius that became pilgrimage sites for healing
d: The 60 treatises that make up the Hippocratic Writings
Battlefield hospitals used during the Trojan War
Schools of human anatomy founded by Galen in Rome
bank.why: Temples dedicated to Asclepius were called Asclepieia.
bank.hint: The name comes from the healer.

bank.q: Which statement best describes healing at Asclepius' sanctuaries?
bank.a: Divine healing and practical care coexisted
d: Only prayer was allowed; practical treatment was forbidden
The sanctuaries were used only for dissection
bank.why: Practitioners gave practical treatments at religious sites; Greek medicine did not fully separate spirituality from physical medicine.

bank.q: Which list gives the four humors?
bank.a: Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile
d: Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and white bile
Air, water, fire and the earth element
Yin, yang, qi and the five elements
bank.why: The four humors are blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.

bank.q: Which humor corresponds to the sanguine temperament (cheerful, energetic, optimistic)?
bank.why: Blood = sanguine = air = cheerful, energetic, optimistic.
bank.hint: "Sanguine" comes from the Latin word for blood.

bank.q: Black bile corresponds to which temperament?
bank.a: Melancholic: analytical, thoughtful, prone to sadness
bank.why: Black bile = melancholic = earth.

bank.q: A person described as passionate, ambitious and easily angered was thought to be dominated by which humor?
bank.why: Yellow bile = choleric = fire.

bank.q: A Greek physician describes a patient as calm, level-headed and deliberate. Which humor would he say dominates?
bank.why: Phlegm (phlegmatic) = calm, level-headed, deliberate.

bank.q: Which element is paired with phlegm?
bank.why: Blood = air, phlegm = water, yellow bile = fire, black bile = earth.

bank.q: Which element is paired with blood (sanguine)?
bank.why: Blood is paired with air.
bank.hint: Light and lively, like the temperament.

bank.q: Which element is paired with black bile?
bank.why: Black bile (melancholic) is paired with earth.

bank.q: Which element is paired with yellow bile?
bank.why: Yellow bile (choleric) is paired with fire.

bank.q: According to the Four Humors Theory, what causes disease?
bank.a: An imbalance of the humors from poor diet, climate or lifestyle
d: Microorganisms entering the body through wounds
Demons such as Lamashtu attacking the patient
Poisonous gases rising from rotting matter
bank.why: Disease occurred when the four humors became unbalanced.

bank.q: In humoral medicine, what was treatment designed to do?
d: Kill the germs causing the infection
Target one organ with a chemical
bank.why: Treatments counteracted imbalances to restore equilibrium.

bank.q: Who is widely celebrated as the "Father of Medicine"?
bank.why: Hippocrates (c. 460 to 370 BCE) is called the Father of Medicine.
bank.hint: The famous Oath is named after him.

bank.q: When did Hippocrates live?
bank.why: Hippocrates lived c. 460 to 370 BCE.
bank.hint: Before the Common Era, in the 5th to 4th centuries.

bank.q: How did Hippocrates change medicine?
bank.a: He taught natural causes of illness, observation, prognosis and ethics
d: He taught that disease powers come from the stars and planets
He showed that the liver produces and consumes the blood
He taught that illness is caused by gods, demons and spirits
bank.why: Hippocrates rejected superstitious explanations, taught natural causes, and prioritized observation, prognosis and medical ethics.

bank.q: Which Greek physician practiced during the Roman period and wrote works that stayed authoritative for over a thousand years?
bank.why: Galen (129 to c. 216 CE) expanded Hippocratic principles and studied anatomy and physiology.

bank.q: What did Galen do with Hippocratic medicine?
bank.a: He expanded it through studies of anatomy and physiology
d: He rejected it in favor of healing in the temples
He translated it into Sanskrit for Indian physicians
He replaced it with chemical remedies like mercury
bank.why: Galen expanded heavily on Hippocratic principles and studied anatomy and physiology.

bank.q: When did Galen live?
bank.why: Galen lived from 129 to about 216 CE. (140 to 208 CE is Hua Tuo.)
bank.hint: Second to early third century CE.

bank.q: In Greek medicine, what is "prognosis"?
bank.a: Forecasting the likely course and outcome of an illness
d: Documenting individual patient files for shared knowledge
Monitoring symptoms closely to guide the diagnosis
Restoring the balance between the four humors
bank.why: Prognosis means forecasting the course and outcome. Case histories document files; clinical observation monitors symptoms.

bank.q: What was the purpose of Greek medical case histories?
bank.a: Documenting individual patients to build shared knowledge
d: Predicting the probable outcome of an illness
Recording the prayers and dreams of pilgrims at Epidaurus
Listing each patient's dominant humor and temperament
bank.why: Medical case histories documented individual patients to build shared knowledge.

bank.q: "Careful monitoring of patient symptoms and condition changes to guide diagnosis" defines which Greek concept?
bank.why: That is clinical observation.

bank.q: Which source contains some of the earliest written accounts of Greek medicine, including battlefield wound care in the Trojan War?
bank.why: Homer's Iliad describes battlefield wound care during the Trojan War.

bank.q: Which statement about the Hippocratic Writings is correct?
bank.a: About 60 treatises not written directly by Hippocrates
d: A single book written by Hippocrates himself
The source of the phrase "First, do no harm"
Seven books on human anatomy and dissection
bank.why: The Hippocratic Writings are around 60 treatises on diagnostics, biology and treatment, not written directly by Hippocrates.
bank.hint: The author is not who you'd expect.

bank.q: What is notable about the phrase "First, do no harm"?
bank.a: It is not in the original Hippocratic Oath
d: It was first written by Galen in Rome
It comes from the Ebers Papyrus of Egypt
It was the personal motto of Paracelsus
bank.why: The Hippocratic Oath outlines a doctor's duties, but "First, do no harm" is not in the original text.

bank.q: A physician visits a feverish patient daily, writes down every change and predicts how many days the illness will last. Which tradition does this reflect?
bank.why: Close observation, documenting symptoms and prognosis are the core of Hippocratic medicine.

bank.q: What does "Ayurveda" mean?
bank.why: Ayurveda means "the science of life."

bank.q: Roughly how long ago was Ayurveda developed?
bank.why: Ayurveda was developed over 3,000 years ago. (At least 23 centuries is how long TCM has lasted.)

bank.q: Ayurveda integrates which elements?
bank.a: Holistic health, herbalism, internal medicine and surgery
d: Acupuncture, qi, yin-yang and the five-element cycles
Chemistry, mercury, sulfur and the study of poisons
Germ theory, laboratory vaccines and antiseptic surgery
bank.why: Ayurveda integrates holistic health, herbalism, internal medicine and early surgical practices.
bank.hint: The only option from ancient India.

bank.q: Which statement about Ayurveda is true according to the lecture?
bank.a: It is still practiced and remains important in India
d: It disappeared completely after the Renaissance
It was created by Hua Tuo in the 2nd century AD
It ignores diet and lifestyle as causes of illness
bank.why: Ayurveda remains an important traditional healthcare system in India.

bank.q: According to the comparison slide, how did Ayurveda maintain health?
d: By balancing yin, yang and qi
bank.why: India: Ayurveda maintained health by balancing the three doshas.

bank.q: Who is known as the Father of Indian Medicine, or Father of Ayurveda?
bank.why: Charaka wrote the Charaka Samhita and is called the Father of Indian Medicine / Ayurveda.
bank.hint: His Samhita is about internal medicine.

bank.q: Which contributions are credited to Charaka?
bank.a: Diagnostic reasoning, herbal pharmacology and preventive health
d: Writing the first comprehensive treatise on surgery
Plastic surgery, including reconstructing the nose
Treating the Buddha and King Bimbisara of Magadha
bank.why: Charaka pioneered diagnostic reasoning, herbal pharmacology and prevention through diet, digestion and mental well-being.

bank.q: Who is celebrated as both the "Father of Surgery" and the "Father of Plastic Surgery"?
bank.why: Sushruta wrote the Sushruta Samhita, the earliest known comprehensive treatise on surgery.

bank.q: Where did Sushruta practice?
bank.why: Sushruta practiced in the ancient city of Kashi, today called Varanasi.
bank.hint: The city also has a modern name.

bank.q: Jivaka Komarabhacca is best known as the personal doctor to whom?
bank.a: The Buddha, King Bimbisara and the Sangha
d: Pharaoh Djoser and the royal court of Egypt
Four French kings and their royal families
The warlord Cao Cao and his generals
bank.why: Jivaka was the personal doctor to the Buddha, King Bimbisara and the early Buddhist monastic community.

bank.q: What is the main focus of the Charaka Samhita?
bank.why: Charaka Samhita = internal medicine; Sushruta Samhita = surgery.

bank.q: The Sushruta Samhita is recognized as one of the earliest foundational treatises on what?
bank.why: Sushruta Samhita = surgery (Shalya Tantra) and anatomy.
bank.hint: Think of the Father of Surgery.

bank.q: How did the Charaka Samhita change medical thought in ancient India?
bank.a: It moved it from supernatural explanations toward rational diagnosis
d: It replaced herbal remedies with chemical ones like mercury
It brought the Greek four humors theory into India
It banned surgery in favor of prayer and chanting
bank.why: The Charaka Samhita shifted Indian medicine toward rational diagnosis.

bank.q: When was the Charaka Samhita compiled?
d: 3rd millennium BCE, under the Yellow Emperor
bank.why: Charaka Samhita: 4th century BCE to 2nd century CE. Sushruta Samhita: c. 600 BCE to 500 CE.
bank.hint: It ends in the 2nd century CE.

bank.q: Around when was the Sushruta Samhita compiled?
bank.why: The Sushruta Samhita was compiled around 600 BCE to 500 CE.
bank.hint: It starts earlier and ends later than the Charaka Samhita.

bank.q: In what language were the Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita written?
bank.why: Both are foundational Sanskrit texts of Ayurveda.

bank.q: Turmeric's major compound, studied for anti-inflammatory activity, is what?
bank.why: Turmeric's major compound is curcumin.
bank.hint: Not a poison and not a disinfectant.

bank.q: Which herb has a long history in South Asian medicine and has shown antimicrobial activity in lab research?
bank.why: Neem has shown antimicrobial activity in laboratory research.

bank.q: Modern research has linked some of garlic's compounds to which effects?
bank.why: Garlic: antimicrobial and cardiovascular effects.

bank.q: In Ayurvedic holistic diagnostics, what did physicians assess?
bank.a: Pulse, tongue, eyes, bodily fluids, appearance and mental state
d: Only the balance of the four humors in the blood
Chest sounds heard through a hollow wooden tube
The patient's zodiac sign and the position of the stars
bank.why: Ayurveda evaluated the whole patient: pulse, tongue, eyes, fluids, appearance and mental state.

bank.q: Which practices did Ayurveda use for mind-body integration?
bank.why: Mind-body integration used yoga, meditation and chanting.

bank.q: Ayurveda's preventive lifestyle emphasized which habits?
bank.a: Daily routines, nutrition, hygiene, exercise and sleep
d: Fasting, bloodletting with leeches and purging
Pilgrimages to temples and sacred dream healing
Daily tonics made of mercury, sulfur and salt
bank.why: Ayurveda prevented disease through routine, nutrition, hygiene, exercise and sleep.

bank.q: What did Ayurvedic medical ethics require of physicians?
d: Swearing the Hippocratic Oath before practicing
Performing public human dissections for students
Wearing blood-stained coats as badges of honor
bank.why: Ayurveda mandated strict professional conduct.

bank.q: An ancient Indian healer is preparing to repair a wound and set a broken bone using specialized instruments. Whose text would be the best guide?
bank.why: The Sushruta Samhita documented surgical techniques, wound care, fracture treatment and specialized instruments.

bank.q: An Ayurvedic physician is treating a patient's chronic digestive illness with diet changes and herbs, without surgery. Which text matches this best?
bank.why: The Charaka Samhita is the foundational text of Ayurvedic internal medicine, including diet and digestion.

bank.q: According to the lecture, Traditional Chinese Medicine has lasted for at least how long?
bank.why: TCM has lasted at least 23 centuries.
bank.hint: A little over two thousand years.

bank.q: What is the central aim of Traditional Chinese Medicine?
bank.a: To restore or maintain the body's yin-yang balance
d: To restore balance among the four bodily humors
To drive away demons with rituals and amulets
To kill germs with chemicals such as carbolic acid
bank.why: TCM aims to restore or maintain yin-yang balance.

bank.q: What does "Huangdi Neijing" mean?
bank.why: Huang = Yellow, Di = Emperor, Nei = Inner, Jing = Classic or Canon.

bank.q: Which is the foundational text of Traditional Chinese Medicine?
bank.why: The Huangdi Neijing is the foundational TCM text, linking health to nature's rhythms and balance.

bank.q: In "Huangdi Neijing", what does "Jing" mean?
bank.why: Huang = Yellow, Di = Emperor, Nei = Inner, Jing = Classic, Canon or Warp thread.
bank.hint: The last word of the title.

bank.q: In "Huangdi Neijing", what does "Nei" mean?
bank.why: Nei = Inner / Internal.

bank.q: Which part of the Huangdi Neijing, "Basic Questions", covers core theories, philosophy, causes of illness and diagnosis?
bank.why: Suwen = Basic Questions; Lingshu = Spiritual Pivot.

bank.q: Which part of the Huangdi Neijing, the "Spiritual Pivot", covers anatomy, acupuncture channels and needle techniques?
bank.why: Lingshu = Spiritual Pivot (anatomy and acupuncture).

bank.q: A TCM student wants to learn where to place acupuncture needles. Which part of the Huangdi Neijing should they study?
bank.why: The Lingshu covers acupuncture channels and needle techniques.

bank.q: Which qualities belong to yang?
bank.why: Yang = active, masculine, hard, bright; yin = passive, feminine, soft, dark.

bank.q: Which qualities belong to yin?
bank.why: Yin = passive, feminine, soft, dark.
bank.hint: The opposite of bright and active.

bank.q: In TCM, when is the human body healthy?
bank.a: When there is a dynamic balance between yin and yang
d: When the humors are drained by bloodletting
When all qi is held still
bank.why: Health is a dynamic balance between the two complementary forces.

bank.q: In TCM, what is "qi"?
bank.why: Qi (energy) is one of the key TCM concepts linked to the Yellow Emperor.

bank.q: What does "Wuxing" refer to?
bank.a: The Five Elements, linking nature and the human body
d: The two complementary forces of yin and yang
The vital energy that flows through the body
Hua Tuo's herbal anesthetic taken with wine
bank.why: Wuxing = the Five Elements.
bank.hint: It is a set of elements.

bank.q: In the Five Elements, what is the creation cycle?
bank.a: Each element nourishes the next element
d: The elements control or balance each other
Yin turns into yang every season
bank.why: Creation cycle = each element nourishes the next; controlling cycle = the elements control or balance each other.

bank.q: In the Five Elements, what is the controlling cycle?
bank.a: The elements control or balance each other
d: Each element nourishes the next element
Qi flows only from the heart
Heat is used to burn tissue
bank.why: Controlling cycle = the elements control or balance each other.
bank.hint: The elements keep each other in check.

bank.q: How does the lecture define acupuncture?
bank.a: Inserting thin, sterile needles at specific points on the body
d: Burning tissue with a hot iron to stop the bleeding
Drinking an herbal mixture with wine before surgery
Draining blood with leeches at specific points
bank.why: Acupuncture inserts thin, sterile needles at specific points.

bank.q: TCM herbal medicine uses which kinds of substances?
d: Only the leaves of medicinal plants
Only synthetic chemicals made in labs
Only metals such as mercury and iron
bank.why: TCM herbal medicine uses plant, animal and mineral substances to restore balance.

bank.q: What was Mafeisan?
bank.a: The world's earliest documented herbal anesthetic
d: The foundational text of Chinese medicine
A key acupuncture point on the stomach channel
The five-element creation and controlling cycle
bank.why: Mafeisan, created by Hua Tuo in the 2nd century AD, is the earliest documented herbal anesthetic.

bank.q: Who created Mafeisan?
bank.why: Hua Tuo, a TCM physician and surgeon (140 to 208 CE), created Mafeisan.

bank.q: How was Mafeisan administered?
bank.why: Mafeisan was taken orally with wine.

bank.q: In which century was Mafeisan created?
bank.why: Hua Tuo created Mafeisan in the 2nd century AD.

bank.q: Why was the original Mafeisan formula lost?
bank.a: Hua Tuo was executed and his texts destroyed
d: The Yellow Emperor kept the recipe secret
Daoist priests banned it as a dangerous poison
It was written only on fragile clay tablets
bank.why: The formula was lost after Hua Tuo's execution and the destruction of his texts.

bank.q: Which ingredients are suspected to have been in Mafeisan?
bank.why: Suspected ingredients: cannabis, monkshood (aconitine) or datura.
bank.hint: Plants with strong effects on the nervous system.

bank.q: Who executed Hua Tuo?
bank.why: Hua Tuo was executed by the warlord Cao Cao.

bank.q: When did Hua Tuo live?
bank.why: Hua Tuo lived 140 to 208 CE. (129 to c. 216 CE is Galen.)
bank.hint: His anesthetic dates to the 2nd century AD.

bank.q: Who is Xuanyuan Huangdi?
bank.a: The Yellow Emperor, linked to the Huangdi Neijing
